standard.title: The Australian Home Front in the Second World War
standard.description: the effects of the Second World War, with a particular emphasis on the continuities and changes on the Australian home front, such as the changing roles of women and First Nations Australians, and the use of wartime government controls
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the effects of World War One on the Australian home front, including conscription debates, the changing roles of women, and the impact of the war on Australian society.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate continuities and changes on the Australian home front during the Second World War, including the changing roles of women and First Nations Australians, the impact of wartime government controls, and local and national effects of the war.

nodes.label: Conscription and wartime government controls
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the introduction of conscription in WWII Australia and explain how wartime government controls affected individual rights and freedoms.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the introduction of conscription through the Citizen Military Forces (contrasting with WWI policy) and explain at least two effects of the National Security Act 1939 on individual rights.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss conscription through the Citizen Military Forces as a change from WWI voluntary enlistment; describe the effects of the National Security Act 1939 — censorship of the media, detention of Japanese, German and Italian residents, banning of groups opposed to the war on political or religious grounds, and 'manpower controls' over the workforce.
wider: Investigate the experiences of Japanese, German and Italian Australians interned under the National Security Act, examining the tension between wartime security imperatives and civil liberties through personal accounts and government records
Compare the conscription debate in WWII Australia with the WWI conscription referendums, examining what changed and what remained contested in Australian attitudes toward compulsory military service

response_modes.reason: The National Security Act's effects are often taught only through censorship. Widening to include detention of enemy aliens and manpower controls gives a more complete picture of how wartime emergency powers operated across different groups.

success_criteria: Explain how the introduction of conscription in WWII differed from WWI policy
Describe at least two ways the National Security Act 1939 restricted individual rights and freedoms
Identify at least one group whose freedoms were specifically restricted by wartime controls and explain the government's stated justification

nodes.label: Women's roles — change and continuity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the changing roles of women on the Australian home front during WWII, contrasting wartime changes with the continuities of women's roles before and after the war.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two new roles women took on during the war and explain whether these represented lasting change or temporary wartime adjustment.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the effects of WWII on women's roles: women in military auxiliary services (WAAAF, AWAS, WRANS), the Women's Land Army, factory work and industrial labour; contrast these wartime changes with the continuities — most women returned to domestic roles after the war; analyse what this pattern of change and reversion reveals about the limits of wartime social transformation.
wider: Examine the experiences of specific women in wartime auxiliary services through personal accounts or oral histories, analysing how individual women navigated the tension between new opportunities and social expectations
Compare the wartime roles of women in Australia with those in Britain or the USA, evaluating similarities and differences in how governments mobilised and then demobilised women's labour

Investigate the long-term effects of wartime women's employment on postwar attitudes to women's workforce participation, examining whether WWII was a genuine turning point in women's rights or a temporary disruption to traditional roles
nodes.hinge_reason: The change-and-continuity analytical frame established here (wartime change followed by post-war reversion) is the central analytical structure for K12 (women's movement) and K13 (continuing civil rights efforts). Students who see wartime women's roles only as change — without the continuity dimension — misread the subsequent women's movement as starting from a stronger base than it actually did.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly teach the change-and-continuity framework as a historical concept — distinguishing surface-level changes (new roles during war) from structural continuities (return to domestic roles after war) — before asking students to apply it to women's wartime experience.

success_criteria: Identify at least two new roles women took on during WWII and describe what each involved
Explain the difference between the changes to women's roles during the war and the continuities after it
Use evidence to support a claim about whether WWII was a turning point for women's rights in Australia

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and the war effort
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the barriers First Nations Australians faced in enlisting, explain why the government changed its position, and describe the roles First Nations Australians played in the war effort.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two barriers First Nations Australians faced in enlisting and explain why the Australian Government eventually changed its position on their inclusion in the defence forces.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the barriers to First Nations Australians' enlistment — lack of trust in their loyalty, denial of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander status, fears of disharmony with non-Indigenous men; examine the government's changing position — the critical shortage of soldiers, establishment of the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion in 1941, specialised roles including the Nackeroos and the Northern Territory Special Reconnaissance Unit; examine the changing civilian roles of First Nations men and women — domestic work in hospitals, ammunition stacking, timber cutting, and other industrial roles.
wider: Investigate the experiences of specific First Nations servicemen and women through oral histories and personal accounts, examining how they navigated discrimination within the military and the gap between their wartime service and their post-war treatment by the government

Examine the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion in depth — its formation, its role in defending the Torres Strait, and how its history has been remembered and recognised in Australian military history

Compare the wartime service of First Nations Australians with their post-war legal status, examining the contradiction between their service to the nation and their continuing exclusion from full citizenship rights
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that First Nations Australians were excluded from and then selectively included in the war effort — and then denied post-war rights despite their service — cannot make sense of K09 (causes of the civil rights campaign) or K10 (civil rights individuals and groups). The contradiction between wartime service and continued exclusion is a key driver of the postwar civil rights movement.

response_modes.reason: The government's shifting position on First Nations enlistment is driven by strategic necessity rather than changed values — make this distinction explicit. Students need to understand that inclusion was instrumental, not principled, to understand why civil rights campaigns were still necessary after the war.

Extend beyond male combat roles to include women's civilian contributions and the Torres Strait specifically — both are elaboration-supported contexts that are commonly omitted in favour of the Nackeroos narrative.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The gap between First Nations wartime service and post-war citizenship rights is a powerful case study in the historical concept of contested inclusion — directly relevant to K09–K13 and to broader discussions of how national identity is constructed and contested.
success_criteria: Identify at least two barriers First Nations Australians faced in enlisting and explain the reasoning behind each
Explain why the Australian Government changed its position on including First Nations Australians in the defence forces
Describe at least two roles First Nations Australians played in the war effort — military or civilian

nodes.label: Local and national impacts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the impact of the Second World War at local and national level in Australia, including specific events that brought the war to Australian soil.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two events that brought the war to Australia and explain their impact on Australian society.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the impact of the war at local and national level: the bombing of Darwin, the Japanese submarine attack on Sydney and the sinking of ships off the Australian coast, the 'Battle of Brisbane' (conflict between Australian and US troops), the Cowra breakout, and the Brisbane Line controversy; explain what these events reveal about Australia's vulnerability and the social pressures of wartime.
wider: Investigate the bombing of Darwin in depth — examining its scale (it was a larger attack than Pearl Harbor), the government's initial suppression of information about it, and its long-term place in Australian memory and commemoration

Examine the Cowra breakout as a case study in the treatment of POWs in Australia, comparing it with the treatment of Australian POWs in Japanese camps and analysing what the incident reveals about wartime attitudes to enemy combatants

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the home-front themes — government controls, women's roles, First Nations service — with the concrete reality of the war reaching Australian territory. Use it to bring together the full picture of wartime Australia before moving to K05 (post-war development).

success_criteria: Describe at least two events that brought the Second World War to Australian soil and explain the impact of each
Explain what the bombing of Darwin or the Japanese submarine attack on Sydney reveals about Australia's wartime vulnerability
Describe how at least one local wartime event affected civilian life in Australia
